'''George Robert Price''' (October 16, 1922 – January 6, 1975) was an American [[population genetics|population geneticist]]. Price is often noted for his formulation of the [[Price equation]] in 1967.

Originally a [[physical chemistry|physical chemist]] and later a [[scientific journalism|science journalist]], he moved to [[London]] in 1967, where he worked in [[theoretical biology]] at the [[Galton Laboratory]], making three important contributions:  first, rederiving [[W.D. Hamilton]]'s work on [[kin selection]] with the new Price equation that vindicated [[group selection]]; second, introducing (with [[John Maynard Smith]]) the concept of the [[evolutionarily stable strategy]] (ESS), a central concept in [[game theory]]; and third, formalizing [[Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection]].

Price converted to [[Christianity]] and gave all his possessions to the poor.  Struggling with a [[Hypothyroidism|thyroid condition]] in conditions of great poverty, he grew increasingly depressed<ref name=Heinrich>{{Cite journal |pmc = 419396|year = 2003|last1 = Heinrich|first1 = T. W.|title = Hypothyroidism Presenting as Psychosis: Myxedema Madness Revisited|journal = Primary Care Companion to the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry|volume = 5|issue = 6|pages = 260–266|last2 = Grahm|first2 = G.|pmid = 15213796|doi = 10.4088/pcc.v05n0603}}</ref> and committed suicide.

==Early life==
Price was born in 1922 in the U.S. state of New York.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/health-and-families/healthy-living/george-price-the-altruistic-man-who-died-trying-to-prove-selflessness-doesn-t-exist-a7237866.html|title=George Price: The altruistic man who died trying to prove selflessness doesn't exist|work=The Independent|date=12 September 2016|author=Regnier, Michael}}</ref> His father, an electrician, died when Price was four. His mother was a former theater actress, and the family struggled through the [[Great Depression]].<ref name="Dugatkin-108">{{cite book|last=Dugatkin|first=Lee Alan|title=The Altruism Equation|year=2011|publisher=Princeton University Press|page=108|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t7ydwfwLKc8C&pg=PA108|isbn=978-1400841431}}</ref>

Price attended [[Birch Wathen Lenox School|Birch Wathen School]]<ref name=":0" /> followed by [[Stuyvesant High School]] in [[New York City|New York]]. He graduated with a degree in [[chemistry]] from [[University of Chicago]] in 1943 and received his [[doctorate]] in the subject from the same institution in 1946.<ref name="Dugatkin-108"/>

In 1947 he married Julia Madigan, but their relationship was contentious as George was a [[strong atheism|strong atheist]] while his wife was a practicing [[Roman Catholic]].<ref name="Dugatkin-108"/> They [[divorce]]d in 1955, having had two daughters, Annamarie and Kathleen.

==Career==

===Early career===
Price was a member of the Manhattan Project as a chemist looking into the characteristics of [[plutonium-235]].
Between 1946 and 1948, he was an instructor in chemistry at [[Harvard University]] and consultant to [[Argonne National Laboratory]]. Later, he took a position at [[Bell Laboratories]] to work on the chemistry of transistors.<ref name=":0" /> He then worked as a research associate in [[medicine]] at the [[University of Minnesota]], working on, among other things, [[fluorescence microscopy]] and [[liver perfusion]]. In 1955 and 1956, he published two papers in the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' criticizing the [[pseudoscience|pseudoscientific]] claims of [[extrasensory perception]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1126/science.122.3165.359 | pmid=13246641 | last=Price | first=G.R. | year=1955 | title=Science and the supernatural | journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]  | volume=122 | pages=359–367 | jstor=1750914 | issue=3165|bibcode = 1955Sci...122..359P }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1126/science.123.3184.17 | pmid=13281471 | last=Price | first=G.R. | year=1956 | title=Where is the definitive experiment? | journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume=123 | pages=17–18 | jstor=1750107 | issue=3184|bibcode = 1956Sci...123...17P }}</ref>

Continuing with science journalism, Price tried to write a book titled ''No Easy Way'' about the [[United States]]' [[Cold War]] with the [[Soviet Union]] and the [[People's Republic of China]], but complained that "the world kept changing faster than I could write about it", and so the book was never finished.

From 1961 to 1967, Price was employed by [[IBM]] as a consultant on graphic data processing. In 1966, he was treated for [[thyroid cancer]], but the operation to remove the tumour left his shoulder partially paralysed and left him reliant on [[thyroxine]] medication. With the money from his [[medical insurance]], he moved to the [[United Kingdom]] to start a new life in November 1967.

===In Britain===
[[W.D. Hamilton]] failed to recall when Price first contacted him, but says Price had read Hamilton's 1964 papers on [[kin selection]],<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/0022-5193(64)90038-4 | author-link=W.D. Hamilton | last=Hamilton | first=W.D. | year=1964 | title=The evolution of social behaviour I | journal=[[Journal of Theoretical Biology]] | volume=7 | pmid=5875341 | issue=1 | pages=1–16 | s2cid=5310280 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/0022-5193(64)90039-6 | author-link=W.D. Hamilton | last=Hamilton | first=W.D. | year=1964 | title=The evolution of social behaviour II | journal=[[Journal of Theoretical Biology]] | volume=7 | pmid=5875340 | issue=1 | pages=17–52 }}</ref> and with no training in [[population genetics]] or [[statistics]] devised the Price equation,<ref name="price1972">{{cite journal | doi=10.1111/j.1469-1809.1972.tb00764.x | last=Price | first=G.R. | year=1972 | title=Fisher's ''fundamental theorem'' made clear | journal=[[Annals of Human Genetics]] | volume=36 | issue=2 | pages=129–140 | pmid=4656569| s2cid=20757537 }}</ref> a [[covariance]] equation that generated the change in [[allele frequency]] of a population.<ref>{{cite book | author-link=W.D. Hamilton | last=Hamilton | first=W.D. | year=1996 | title=Narrow Roads of Gene Land, Volume 1 | publisher=[[Oxford University Press]], Oxford | isbn=978-0-7167-4530-3 }}</ref><!-- esp ch5 and ch9 -->  Although the first part of the equation had previously been derived by [[Alan Robertson (geneticist)|Alan Robertson]]<ref name="robertson1966">{{cite journal | doi=10.1017/S0003356100037752 | last=Robertson | first=Alan | year=1966 | title=A Mathematical Model of the Culling Process in Dairy Cattle | journal=[[Animal Production]] | volume=8 | pages=95–108 }}</ref> and [[C. C. Li]],<ref name="li1967">{{cite journal | last=Li | first=C.C. |date=April 1967 | title=Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=214 | issue=5087  | pages=505–506 | doi=10.1038/214505a0 | pmid=6032884 |bibcode = 1967Natur.214..505L | s2cid=4182121 }}</ref> its second component allowed it to be applied to all levels of selection, [[meiotic drive]], traditional [[natural selection]] with an extension into [[inclusive fitness]] and [[group selection]].

===Conversion to Christianity===
On 6 June 1970,<ref name=":0">[[Oren Harman]] (2010) ''The Price of Altruism: George Price and the Search for the Origins of Kindness'', New York : [[W.W. Norton]], {{ISBN|978-0-393-06778-1}}</ref> Price had a religious experience and became an ardent scholar of the [[New Testament]]. He believed that there had been too many [[coincidence]]s in his life. In particular, he wrote a lengthy essay titled ''The Twelve Days of Easter'', arguing that the calendar of events surrounding [[Jesus]] of [[Nazareth]]'s death in [[Easter|Easter Week]] was actually slightly longer. Later he turned away from [[Biblical scholarship]] and instead dedicated his life to community work, helping the needy of [[North London]].

===Other work in evolutionary theory===
Price developed a new interpretation of [[Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection]], the Price equation, which has now been accepted as the best interpretation of a formerly enigmatic result.<ref name="price1972"/>  He wrote what is still widely held to be the best mathematical, biological and evolutionary representation of [[altruism]]. He also pioneered the application of [[game theory]] to evolutionary biology, in a co-authored 1973 paper with John Maynard Smith.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1038/246015a0 | author-link=John Maynard Smith | last1=Maynard Smith | first1=J. | last2=Price | first2=G.R. | year=1973 | title=The logic of animal conflict | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=246 | pages=15–18 | issue=5427 | bibcode=1973Natur.246...15S| s2cid=4224989 }}</ref> Furthermore, Price reasoned that in the same way as an organism may sacrifice itself and further its genes ([[altruism]]) an organism may sacrifice itself to eliminate others of the same species if it enabled closely related organisms to better propagate their related genes. This negative altruism was described in a paper published by W. D. Hamilton and is termed [[Hamiltonian spite]].

Price's 'mathematical' theory of altruism reasons that organisms are more likely to show altruism toward each other as they become more genetically similar to each other. Thus, in a species that requires two parents to reproduce, an organism is most likely to show altruistic behavior to a biological parent, full sibling, or direct offspring. The reason for this is that each of these relatives' genetic makeup contains (on average in the case of siblings) 50% of the genes that are found in the original organism. So if the original organism dies as a result of an altruistic act it can still manage to propagate its full genetic heritage as long as two or more of these close relatives are saved. Consequently, an organism is less likely to show altruistic behavior to a biological grandparent, grandchild, aunt/uncle, niece/nephew or [[half-sibling]] (each carry one-fourth of the genes found in the original organism); and even less likely to show altruism to a [[first cousin]] (carrying one-eighth of the genes found in the original organism). The theory then asserts that the further genetically removed two organisms are from each other, the less likely they are to show altruism to each other.

===Helping the homeless===
Price grew increasingly depressed by the implications of his equation. As part of an attempt to prove his theory right or wrong, he began showing an ever-increasing amount (in both quality and quantity) of [[random kindness]] to complete strangers. In this way, he dedicated the latter part of his life to helping the [[homeless]], often inviting homeless people to live in his house. Sometimes, when the people in his house became a distraction, he slept in his office at the [[Galton Laboratory]]. He also gave up everything to help alcoholics; yet as he helped them steal his belongings, he increasingly fell into depression.<ref>Interviews with Price's biographer and daughter in "All Watched Over By Machines of Loving Grace" by Adam Curtis: [https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1958138/ The Monkey in the Machine and the Machine in the Monkey]</ref>{{Page needed|date=August 2024|time=yes}}<!-- Removed a reference to a Vimeo video (https://vimeo.com/80799354) because it was taken down due to infringing on BBC's copyright. -->

He was eventually evicted from his rented house owing to a construction project in the area, making him unhappy because he could no longer provide housing for the homeless. He moved to various [[Squatting|squats]] in the North London area, and became depressed over Christmas, 1974.<ref>Harman O. 2020 When science mirrors life: on the origins of the Price equation. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 375: 20190352. http://dx.doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2019.0352</ref>

==Death==
Possibly due to the long-term complications of his thyroid treatment,<ref name=Heinrich/> Price died by suicide on January 6, 1975, by cutting his [[carotid artery]] with a pair of nail scissors. His body was identified by his close colleague, W.D. Hamilton.<ref name="AndrewBrown2000">{{cite book | last= Brown| first= Andrew |author-link=Andrew Brown (writer)| title= The Darwin Wars: The Scientific Battle for the Soul of Man| year = 2000| publisher= [[Touchstone Books]]| location= London |isbn= 978-0-684-85145-7| page= 1}}</ref>

A memorial service was held for Price in [[Euston, Suffolk|Euston]]. The only persons present from academia were Hamilton and Maynard Smith, the other few mourners being those who had come to know him through his community work. He is buried in [[St Pancras and Islington Cemetery|St Pancras Cemetery]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Harman | first=O. | year=2010 | title=The Price of Altruism: George Price and the Search for the Origins of Kindness |publisher  = W. W. Norton & Company}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Price's contributions were largely overlooked for 20 years; he had worked in [[theoretical biology]] for only a short time and was not very thorough in publishing papers. This has changed in recent years. An article by James Schwartz published in 2000<ref name="Schwartz">{{cite journal | url=http://www.linguafranca.com/0007/altruist.html | title=Death of an Altruist. Was the man who found the selfless gene too good for this world? | author=Schwartz, James | journal=[[Lingua Franca (magazine)|Lingua Franca]] | date=July–August 2000 | volume=10 | issue=5 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001018225623/https://linguafranca.com/0007/altruist.html | archive-date= October 18, 2000 |url-status=dead }}</ref> was the beginning of the historical redress. In 2010, [[Oren Harman]]'s [[Los Angeles Times Book Prize#Science and technology|LA Times Book Prize]] winning biography, ''The Price of Altruism: George Price and the Search for the Origins of Kindness'' was published, and has received major attention, finally bringing Price and his story to the general public. A stage play about Price, ''The Altruists'' by Craig Baxter, won the fourth [[Scientists, Technologists and Artists Generating Exploration|STAGE]] International Script Competition.<ref name="STAGE">{{cite web | url=http://www.stage.ucsb.edu/competition/winners/fourth/the_altruists.php | title=THE ALTRUISTS, by Craig Baxter. Winner of the 4th STAGE International Script Competition | publisher=The Regents of the University of California | work=STAGE - Scientists, Technologists and Artists Generating Exploration | date=April 1, 2015 | access-date=November 21, 2019 | archive-date=25 April 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425091902/http://www.stage.ucsb.edu/competition/winners/fourth/the_altruists.php | url-status=dead }}</ref> On 29 March 2016, Farnworth's play ''Calculating Kindness'' opened for a sold-out three-week run at the Camden People's Theatre.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://nautil.us//blog/how-discovering-an-equation-for-altruism-cost-george-price-everything|title=''How Discovering an Equation for Altruism Cost George Price Everything''|access-date=25 June 2017|archive-date=24 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170624013422/http://nautil.us/blog/how-discovering-an-equation-for-altruism-cost-george-price-everything|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Mosaic">{{cite web | url=https://mosaicscience.com/story/George-Price-altruism-equation | title=The man who gave himself away - How discovering an equation for altruism cost George Price everything | publisher=[[Wellcome Trust]] | work=Mosaic | date=13 September 2016 | access-date=November 21, 2019 | author=Regnier, Michael }}</ref>

==In media==
*The story of Price's equation, its application to altruism, and the profound effects this supposedly had on its discoverer's life were featured in an episode of ''[[Dark Matters: Twisted But True]]'', in a segment entitled "Killed by Kindness".
*Similar coverage, both of Price's contributions to studies of altruism and his efforts to disprove the supposed selfishness of altruism, was discussed in "The Good Show" episode of the NPR series ''[[Radiolab]]'' in December 2010.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Good Show |url=http://www.radiolab.org/story/103951-the-good-show/ |website=Radiolab Podcasts {{!}} WNYC Studios |access-date=28 October 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
*The life and work of Price and his work with Bill Hamilton is the central theme of the third and final documentary of the series ''[[All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace (TV series)#Part 3. 'The Monkey in the Machine and the Machine in the Monkey'|All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace]]'' by [[Adam Curtis]] and includes an interview with his daughter Kathleen.
*The life story of George R. Price was dramatized in 2010 by Craig Baxter, whose play ''The Altruists'' won the S.T.A.G.E. (Scientists, Technologists and Artists Generating Exploration) International Playwriting Competition in that year;<ref name="STAGE"/> and again in 2016 by Lydia Adetunji as a play titled ''Calculating Kindness''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davis |first1=Nicola |title=The man who proved that altruism is selfish |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2016/mar/13/george-davis-altruism-selfish-play-calculating-kindness |access-date=29 October 2026 |work=The Guardian |date=13 March 2016}}</ref>
*Northern Irish singer songwriter [[Joshua Burnside]] wrote about Price and his fate in his song 'George Price'.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kS52xwVHmho|title = Joshua Burnside 'George Price' (Live)|website = [[YouTube]]}}</ref>
*A 2025 episode of [[Tim Harford]]'s [[Cautionary Tales (podcast)|''Cautionary Tales'' podcast]] features Price.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pushkin.fm/podcasts/cautionary-tales/the-man-who-solved-kindness|title = The Man who Solved Kindness |website = Cautionary Tales}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
The Papers of George R Price are housed at the [[British Library]]. The papers can be accessed through the British Library catalogue.<ref>[http://searcharchives.bl.uk/IAMS_VU2:IAMS032-001993204 The Papers of George R Price]{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, archives and manuscripts catalogue, the British Library.
